question: A 14-year-old girl comes to the physician for exertional leg pain. The pain began last week when she started jogging to lose weight. She is at the 5th percentile for height and 80th percentile for weight. Physical examination shows a broad neck with bilateral excess skin folds that extend to the shoulders, as well as a low-set hairline and ears. There is an increased carrying angle when she fully extends her arms at her sides. Pulses are palpable in all extremities; lower leg pulses are delayed. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "14-year-old girl with exertional leg pain" -> "obesity indicated by weight at 80th percentile" -> "possible underlying genetic condition" -> "broad neck and excess skin folds suggest Turner syndrome" -> "Turner syndrome commonly associated with ovarian dysgenesis" -> "most likely additional finding is ovarian dysgenesis" -> 85%

CHAIN: "14-year-old girl with exertional leg pain" -> "delayed lower leg pulses" -> "suggests possible vascular issues" -> "Turner syndrome can be associated with cardiovascular anomalies" -> "mitral valve prolapse is a known association" -> "possible additional finding is mitral valve prolapse" -> 75%

enhanced_information: The 14-year-old girl presents with features suggestive of Turner syndrome, including a broad neck, low-set ears, and delayed lower leg pulses. Turner syndrome is commonly associated with ovarian dysgenesis, which is a well-established finding in affected individuals. While absent uterus is also a possibility, it is less definitive than ovarian dysgenesis in this context. Mitral valve prolapse is associated with Turner syndrome but is not as directly linked to the physical findings presented. Triphalangeal thumb is a rare finding and not a common association. Horseshoe adrenal gland is not typically associated with Turner syndrome. Therefore, the most likely additional finding in this patient is ovarian dysgenesis, supported by the consensus that it is a common manifestation of Turner syndrome.

Turner syndrome is commonly associated with ovarian dysgenesis, leading to primary amenorrhea and infertility.
